claim: Positive: V/sigma increases with relaxation time — GCs with longer relaxation times (also the more massive ones) show stronger internal rotation. Presented as the paper's headline correlation, interpreted as primordial rotation surviving longer where relaxation is slow; no formal correlation coefficient quoted, sample of 51 GCs (11 with >3-sigma rotation, V/sigma ~ 0.08-0.51).
source: Bianchini et al. 2018, MNRAS 481, 2125 (arXiv:1806.02580), 'The internal rotation of globular clusters revealed by Gaia DR2'

claim: Positive: more massive GCs display stronger internal rotation (mass and relaxation time co-vary in their sample). Qualitative trend, no coefficient given.

Positive: internal rotation strength correlates with relaxation time; interpreted as central rotation being a relic of formation that is gradually erased by two-body relaxation. Based on 22 GCs (13 with >3-sigma rotation); trend reported, no coefficient.
source: Kamann et al. 2018, MNRAS 473, 5591 (arXiv:1710.07257), 'A stellar census in globular clusters with MUSE'

claim: Positive: rotation strength is linked to ellipticity — more rotating clusters are more flattened; explicitly stated to confirm earlier findings (Fabricius 2014). Trend, no coefficient.

Positive and described as a tight correlation: central rotation amplitude correlates with outer ellipticity, taken as evidence that rotation (not the Galactic tidal field) drives the flattening. Rotation detected in all 11 clusters observed; correlation qualitative/tight but no numeric coefficient.
source: Fabricius et al. 2014, ApJL 787, L26 (arXiv:1405.1722), 'Central rotations of Milky Way Globular Clusters' (VIRUS-W)

claim: Positive and described as tight: central rotation amplitude correlates with published central velocity dispersion, implying more massive/higher-dispersion clusters rotate more strongly. Qualitative 'tight' correlation, no coefficient.

Weak positive: rotation strength (fraction of kinetic energy in rotation, xi) weakly correlates with half-mass radius; among the largest correlation probabilities but still below 3-sigma significance. Sample of 62 GCs, 15 with clear rotation.
source: Sollima, Baumgardt & Hilker 2019, MNRAS 485, 1460 (arXiv:1902.05895), 'The eye of Gaia on globular clusters kinematics: internal rotation'

claim: Weak positive: xi weakly correlates with half-mass relaxation time — GCs with longer relaxation times rotate faster; below 3-sigma. Consistent in direction with Bianchini 2018 and Kamann 2018.

Negative (anticorrelation): rotation strength xi anticorrelates with the tidal destruction rate — clusters undergoing fast destruction have lost much of their original angular momentum. Trend, below 3-sigma given small sample.
None: explicitly find NO link between rotation and flattening, contradicting Fabricius et al. 2014 and Kamann et al. 2018. (No significant correlation with mass or metallicity reported either.)

Positive: rotation-to-dispersion ratio A_rot/sigma_0 increases with metallicity — metal-rich clusters rotate more. Reported as a significant correlation but weaker than the horizontal-branch dependence and 'unlikely to be the sole parameter'; based on ~25 GCs.
source: Bellazzini et al. 2012, A&A 538, A18 (as discussed/confirmed in Kacharov et al. 2014, A&A 567, A69, arXiv:1406.1552)

claim: Strong correlation: GCs with blue HBs are slower rotators while those with red or extended HBs are faster rotators; described as a very strong correlation and the tightest of the parameters examined (stronger than the metallicity trend).
source: Bellazzini et al. 2012, A&A 538, A18 (via Kacharov et al. 2014, arXiv:1406.1552)

claim: Positive: rotation amplitude is connected to absolute magnitude and central velocity dispersion, both tied to total cluster mass — brighter/more massive clusters rotate more. Reported as a connection, not quantified with a coefficient.
source: Bellazzini et al. 2012, A&A 538, A18 (via Kacharov et al. 2014, arXiv:1406.1552)

claim: None/weak: Bellazzini et al. 2012 (and Lardo et al. 2015) did NOT find a clear correlation between rotation and ellipticity, in contrast to Fabricius 2014 and Kamann 2018 — a point of disagreement in the literature.
source: Bellazzini et al. 2012, A&A 538, A18 / Lardo et al. 2015 (noted in Fabricius et al. 2014 and Kacharov et al. 2014 discussions)

claim: Positive: using V/sigma-vs-ellipticity diagrams they argue higher flattening corresponds to higher V/sigma, concluding rotation is the driving factor of GC ellipticities; NGC 4372 is flagged as an outlier with unusually high rotation for its (very low) metallicity, consistent with a positive rotation-metallicity trend overall.
source: Kacharov et al. 2014, A&A 567, A69 (arXiv:1406.1552), 'A study of rotating globular clusters: NGC 4372'

claim: Not a fitted correlation but a strong claim of prevalence: rotation signals detected in 10 of 11 clusters at a few half-mass radii (Ferraro 2018) and one of the cleanest coherent rotation patterns seen in M5 (Lanzoni 2018); the authors frame residual angular momentum as a relic of formation gradually erased by dynamical (relaxation) evolution — consistent in direction with the rotation vs relaxation-time trend, but no population correlation coefficient is fit.
source: Ferraro et al. 2018, ApJ 860, 50 (MIKiS I, arXiv:1804.08618) and Lanzoni et al. 2018, ApJ 861, 16 (M5, arXiv:1804.10509)
